---
title: "Tool 2 — The CKA Penalty"
subtitle: "Penalise dependence on the group · close the curve hole · read the frontier"
---



*Learn-the-tool track · Lab 2.*

Tool 1 showed the two ways neutrality fails — a dropped attribute leaks back through
proxies, and *linear* removal leaves the curve.  This lab climbs the **penalty
ladder** that fixes both at once: one penalised fit, $\text{loss} +
\lambda\cdot\operatorname{CKA}(\hat y, S)$, that drives the dependence between a
**prediction** and the **group** straight to zero.  CKA — *centered kernel
alignment* — is just a number between 0 and 1 that measures how much two things
depend on each other; 0 means no dependence at all.  The *tool* (penalised fit +
the CKA dependence term) is built once on Rung 1 and reused unchanged; only the
**data grows up under it**, from a toy whose answer you can check by hand to the
real Census basket and the accuracy–fairness frontier it traces.

The CKA penalty is not a new measure — it **reuses the exact double-centering of
the distance-correlation lab** ([Tool 1 · the model-free
ladder](../../dependence/labs/lab-tool1-ladder.qmd)).  There the transform centred
a matrix of *distances*; here it centres a matrix of *kernel similarities*.  Same
$\tilde A_{ij} = A_{ij} - \bar A_{i\cdot} - \bar A_{\cdot j} + \bar A_{\cdot\cdot}$,
a different matrix going in.

**What you will produce:** an accuracy–fairness frontier on real Census income
predictions — a curve that shows, for every bit of the gap between groups you close,
how much accuracy it costs to close it.

---

## 🧪 Rung 1 · Toy — Known Answer

Start where the truth is not in doubt.  `datasets.credit_scores_by_group()` builds
a toy lender whose underlying creditworthiness is **shifted by group**: group 1 sits
a fixed `gap` above group 0, so a model that predicts repayment **inherits that
shift unless something stops it**.  That makes the known answer easy to state by hand:
train a predictor and its output will depend on the group (high CKA); add the
penalty and the dependence must fall to $\approx 0$ — the prediction can no longer
tell the groups apart.

::: {#data-toy .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
d = datasets.credit_scores_by_group(n=600, gap=0.8, seed=0)
score: Float[Array, "n"] = d["score"]                 # legitimate signal (group-shifted)
group: Float[Array, "n"] = d["group"].astype(float)   # the protected attribute, 0/1
repaid: Float[Array, "n"] = d["repaid"].astype(float)  # ground-truth label
gap0 = repaid[group == 1].mean() - repaid[group == 0].mean()
print(f"n={score.size}   repay rate: group0={repaid[group==0].mean():.0%}  "
      f"group1={repaid[group==1].mean():.0%}   group gap={gap0:+.0%}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
n=600   repay rate: group0=47%  group1=67%   group gap=+20%
```
:::
:::


**The tool — penalise the dependence, reusing the dCor double-centering.**  The
algorithm is one objective:

$$
\min_{\hat y}\ \underbrace{\tfrac1n\lVert \hat y - y\rVert^2}_{\text{fit}}
\;+\;\lambda\cdot\underbrace{\operatorname{CKA}(\hat y,\, S)}_{\text{dependence}}
$$

The only new piece is $\operatorname{CKA}$, and it is **not new at all** — it is the
distance-correlation transform with a kernel matrix in place of a distance matrix.
Spelled out with the axes visible, so the shared step is undeniable:

::: {#cka-derivation .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def double_center(M: Float[Array, "n n"]) -> Float[Array, "n n"]:
    """The dCor transform, verbatim: M̃ᵢⱼ = Mᵢⱼ − M̄ᵢ. − M̄.ⱼ + M̄..

    Identical to `centered_distances` in the distance-correlation lab — only the
    matrix going in differs (a kernel gram here, pairwise distances there).
    """
    row_mean = einx.mean("i j -> i", M)              # M̄ᵢ. — row means
    col_mean = einx.mean("i j -> j", M)              # M̄.ⱼ — column means
    A = einx.subtract("i j, i -> i j", M, row_mean)
    A = einx.subtract("i j, j -> i j", A, col_mean)
    return A + M.mean()                              # add back the grand mean M̄..


def cka(x: Float[Array, "n"], y: Float[Array, "n"]) -> float:
    """CKA = ⟨K̃ₓ, K̃ᵧ⟩ / √(⟨K̃ₓ,K̃ₓ⟩⟨K̃ᵧ,K̃ᵧ⟩) — normalised, double-centred gram alignment."""
    Kx = einx.dot("i, j -> i j", x, x)               # linear gram ⟨xᵢ, xⱼ⟩   (n, n)
    Ky = einx.dot("i, j -> i j", y, y)               # linear gram ⟨yᵢ, yⱼ⟩
    Kxc, Kyc = double_center(Kx), double_center(Ky)  # the SAME centering as dCor
    hsic = lambda A, B: float((A * B).mean())         # ⟨Ã, B̃⟩ — the dependence inner product
    denom = np.sqrt(hsic(Kxc, Kxc) * hsic(Kyc, Kyc))
    return hsic(Kxc, Kyc) / denom if denom > 0 else 0.0


# the hand-rolled CKA must match the library's cka_linear — same double-centring:
print(f"cka(score, group)        = {cka(score, group):.4f}   (double-centred gram alignment)")
print(f"cka_linear(score, group) = {cka_linear(score, group):.4f}   (library — identical)")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
cka(score, group)        = 0.2240   (double-centred gram alignment)
cka_linear(score, group) = 0.2240   (library — identical)
```
:::
:::


The penalised fit itself is `fair_fit`: it fits the target, then — for $\lambda>0$ —
removes from the prediction the part that can be explained by the group $S$ (this is
the exact solution to the penalised objective above).  Run it with the penalty off
and on, and read CKA against what we *know* is there:

::: {#toy-fit .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
pred0 = fair_fit(score, repaid, group, mu=0.0)   # plain — inherits the group shift
pred8 = fair_fit(score, repaid, group, mu=8.0)   # penalised — CKA driven down
print(f"plain  (λ=0):  CKA(pred, group) = {cka(pred0, group):.3f}   (depends on the group)")
print(f"penalty(λ=8):  CKA(pred, group) = {cka(pred8, group):.3f}   ← curve gone, groups indistinct")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
plain  (λ=0):  CKA(pred, group) = 0.245   (depends on the group)
penalty(λ=8):  CKA(pred, group) = 0.001   ← curve gone, groups indistinct
```
:::
:::

The known answer holds: the plain predictor inherits the group shift (CKA high, the
two group-mean lines far apart); the penalised one collapses both groups onto the
same prediction band (CKA $\to 0$).  That is the whole tool — minimise
$\text{fit} + \lambda\cdot\operatorname{CKA}(\hat y, S)$, where CKA is the
dependence transform you already met on the distance-correlation ladder.  Now we
feed it data with a hole that the *cheap* fix cannot close.

---

## 🎭 Rung 2 · Toy-Real — A Stylized Market

A group that shifts a prediction by a constant is the easy case — *linear*
neutrality would catch it.  What actually happens in lending is subtler: the target
bends with the sensitive variable (the group label $S$).  `datasets.fair_regression()`
is a simplified stand-in for that — $y = 0.6x + 0.7S + 0.7(S^2-1) + \text{noise}$ —
so $S$ enters the target both as a straight **line** and as a **curve**.  Drop $S$, or subtract the
straight-line part of it, and the $0.7\,S$ term goes — but the $S^2$ curve stays.
That leftover curve is a *proxy hole*: dependence on the group that a linear fix
cannot see, so it leaves the hole wide open.  The CKA penalty, built on the same
kernel that does see curves, closes it.  **Same `fair_fit`, no new code.**

::: {#data-ramp .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
d = datasets.fair_regression(n=600, seed=0)
x, S, y = d["x"], d["s"], d["y"]

# the cheap fix: plain least-squares, then subtract the LINEAR S-projection
Phi = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x, S, S**2 - 1.0])
theta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(Phi, y, rcond=None)
y_plain = Phi @ theta                                  # plain fit — sees the curve
b = np.cov(y_plain, S)[0, 1] / np.var(S)               # OLS slope on S
y_linear = y_plain - b * S                              # linear neutrality: subtract the line

y_cka = fair_fit(x, y, S, mu=8.0)                      # the kernel penalty — same tool as Rung 1

print(f"                Pearson(·,S)   CKA_lin(·,S)   CKA_rbf(·,S)")
print(f"plain            {np.corrcoef(y_plain, S)[0,1]:+.3f}        "
      f"{cka_linear(y_plain, S):.3f}          {cka_rbf(y_plain, S):.3f}")
print(f"linear removal   {np.corrcoef(y_linear, S)[0,1]:+.3f}        "
      f"{cka_linear(y_linear, S):.3f}          {cka_rbf(y_linear, S):.3f}   ← curve survives")
print(f"CKA penalty      {np.corrcoef(y_cka, S)[0,1]:+.3f}        "
      f"{cka_linear(y_cka, S):.3f}          {cka_rbf(y_cka, S):.3f}   ← hole closed")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
                Pearson(·,S)   CKA_lin(·,S)   CKA_rbf(·,S)
plain            +0.439        0.193          0.338
linear removal   -0.001        0.000          0.179   ← curve survives
CKA penalty      +0.133        0.018          0.020   ← hole closed
```
:::
:::

panels = [(y_plain, "plain", COOL), (y_linear, "linear removal", WARM),
          (y_cka, "CKA penalty (λ=8)", GREEN)]
for ax, (pred, ttl, c) in zip(axes, panels):
    ax.scatter(S, pred, s=10, c=c, alpha=0.45, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_title(f"{ttl}\nCKA_rbf={cka_rbf(pred, S):.2f}", fontsize=11)

axes[0].set_ylabel("prediction")

Middle: linear removal flattens the average slope (Pearson → 0) but the U is untouched — the curve is exactly the dependence a linear fix cannot see, so CKA_rbf barely moves. Right: the CKA penalty, using the same kernel that registers the curve, erases it — the cloud is flat in S and CKA_rbf falls near zero. The middle panel is the hole; the right panel is the fix.](lab-tool2-cka-penalty_files/figure-html/fig-ramp-hole-output-1.png){#fig-ramp-hole width=1544 height=466}

:::


Read the three panels left to right: linear removal kills the *correlation* but the
*curve* survives — that leftover $S^2$ dependence is the hole, and CKA$_\text{rbf}$
sees it even though Pearson correlation reads zero.  The penalty closes the hole
because its kernel registers the curve the linear fix is blind to.

So far `fair_fit` solved this in closed form — a teaching stand-in.  In practice you
*train* the same idea on any network, and fair learning has one rule it never breaks:
**the sensitive variable `S` never enters the model — it shapes only the loss.**  The
deployed model takes features alone; `S` changes *how it learns*, not *what it sees*.
Built by hand the mechanism is just three pieces:

1. a network that predicts the target from **features only** (never `S`);
2. the **penalty** $\operatorname{CKA}(\hat y, S)$, written so the network can be trained against it (the optimiser can follow its gradient);
3. the **total loss** $= \text{task loss} + \lambda\cdot\operatorname{CKA}$, added with
   `add_loss` *during training* — so `S` reaches the optimiser but never the inputs.

The leak we fight rides in on a **proxy** — a feature correlated with `S`, the way
`occupation` carries `sex`.  We hand the net a proxy (not `S` itself) and watch the
penalty pull the prediction free of `S` regardless:

::: {#keras-byhand .cell execution_count=8}
`````` {.python .cell-code}
import os
os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "jax"          # set BEFORE importing keras (Keras 3, CPU JAX)
import keras
from keras import layers


def cka_in_graph(pred: Float[Array, "n 1"], s: Float[Array, "n 1"]):
    """RBF CKA(prediction, S) in keras.ops so gradients flow — the SAME kernel that
    caught the curve in Rung 2, and the SAME one `keras-fairkl` uses by default, so
    the by-hand penalty and the package close the same nonlinear leak."""
    def rbf_gram(z: Float[Array, "n 1"]) -> Float[Array, "n n"]:
        z = keras.ops.reshape(z, (-1, 1))
        sq_dist = (z - keras.ops.transpose(z)) ** 2             # (zᵢ − zⱼ)²   pairwise
        sigma2 = keras.ops.median(sq_dist) + 1e-12             # median-heuristic bandwidth
        return keras.ops.exp(-sq_dist / (2.0 * sigma2))        # Kᵢⱼ = exp(−(zᵢ−zⱼ)² / 2σ²)

    def dc(M: Float[Array, "n n"]) -> Float[Array, "n n"]:     # double-centre, in-graph
        return (M - keras.ops.mean(M, 0, keepdims=True)
                  - keras.ops.mean(M, 1, keepdims=True) + keras.ops.mean(M))

    Ac, Bc = dc(rbf_gram(pred)), dc(rbf_gram(s))               # centred RBF grams
    h = lambda P, Q: keras.ops.mean(P * Q)                       # ⟨P̃, Q̃⟩
    return h(Ac, Bc) / keras.ops.sqrt(h(Ac, Ac) * h(Bc, Bc) + 1e-12)


class FairWrap(keras.Model):
    """A minimal `FairModelWrapper`: a base predictor plus a CKA penalty on the loss.

    The base network is called on the **features only**; the sensitive S arrives as
    `q` at fit time and is used *only* inside `add_loss` — never as a model input.
    """
    def __init__(self, base: keras.Model, mu: float):
        super().__init__(); self.base = base; self.mu = mu      # mu = λ, the penalty weight
    def call(self, inputs, training=False):
        x_feat, s = inputs["x"], inputs["q"]                    # q = the sensitive variable
        pred = self.base(x_feat, training=training)             # the model sees ONLY features
        if training and self.mu > 0:
            self.add_loss(self.mu * cka_in_graph(pred, s))      # the penalty rides on the loss
        return pred


# the leak rides in on a PROXY — a feature that carries S (the way occupation carries sex)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
proxy: Float[Array, "n"] = S + 0.3 * rng.standard_normal(len(S))   # corr(proxy, S) ≈ 0.96
X_feat = np.column_stack([x, proxy]).astype("float32")           # features: a clean x + the proxy. NO S.
S_col = S[:, None].astype("float32")                            # S — handed to the loss as q

print(f"{'':16}CKA(pred,S)   R²")
for mu in (0.0, 6.0):
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
    base = keras.Sequential([layers.Dense(32, activation="tanh"),
                             layers.Dense(32, activation="tanh"), layers.Dense(1)])
    model = FairWrap(base, mu)
    model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.01), loss="mse")   # mse = the task loss
    model.fit({"x": X_feat, "q": S_col}, y[:, None].astype("float32"),
              epochs=150, batch_size=128, verbose=0)
    pred = np.asarray(base.predict(X_feat, verbose=0))[:, 0]    # deploy on features alone — S unseen
    r2 = max(1 - np.mean((pred - y) ** 2) / np.var(y), 0.0)
    tag = "plain (λ=0)" if mu == 0 else f"penalty (λ={mu:g})"
    print(f"{tag:16}{cka_rbf(pred, S):.3f}        {r2:.3f}")
``````

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
                CKA(pred,S)   R²
plain (λ=0)     0.273        0.854
penalty (λ=6)   0.034        0.666
```
:::
:::


With the penalty off, the net leans on the proxy and its prediction tracks `S` (CKA
high, accuracy high); with it on, the net is forced to give up the part of the proxy
that carries `S` — CKA falls toward zero at a real accuracy cost.  **`keras-fairkl` is
exactly this, packaged**: it adds the same $\lambda\cdot\operatorname{CKA}(\hat y, S)$
through `add_loss`, takes `S` at `fit` time as `q=`, and never feeds it to your model.

::: {#keras-fairkl .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from fairkl import FairModelWrapper

print(f"{'':16}CKA(pred,S)   R²")
for mu in (0.0, 6.0):
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
    mlp = keras.Sequential([layers.Dense(32, activation="tanh"),
                            layers.Dense(32, activation="tanh"), layers.Dense(1)])
    model = FairModelWrapper(mlp, mu=mu)        # the same mse + λ·CKA(ŷ, S) objective
    model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.01), loss="mse")
    model.fit(X_feat, y[:, None], q=S_col,      # features in; S given only as q, at fit time
              epochs=150, batch_size=128, verbose=0)
    pred = model.predict(X_feat, verbose=0)[:, 0]
    r2 = max(1 - np.mean((pred - y) ** 2) / np.var(y), 0.0)
    print(f"keras-fairkl λ={mu:<4g}{cka_rbf(pred, S):.3f}        {r2:.3f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
                CKA(pred,S)   R²
keras-fairkl λ=0   0.273        0.854
keras-fairkl λ=6   0.028        0.632
```
:::
:::


The by-hand `FairWrap` and the packaged `FairModelWrapper` agree closely — both wrap an
ordinary network, both add an **RBF** $\lambda\cdot\operatorname{CKA}(\hat y, S)$ to the
loss with `S` seen only at fit time, and both drive $\operatorname{CKA}(\hat y, S)$ from
~0.22 down to ~0.02 at the same accuracy cost.  Same kernel, same objective, same
result; the library just spares you re-writing the wrapper.  Only the data escalates
from here.

---

## 📈 Rung 3 · Real — The Full Basket

Now the real panel.  We **reload** the prepared US-Census income data — there is no
cleaning here; the ACS decode, the income-threshold target, and the protected
attribute are built once in
[the income & fairness primer](../../data/06-the-credit-dataset.qmd) — split it into
the standard $(X, y, s)$ pieces, and train a proxy scorecard with `sex`
**dropped**.  The one lab-local step is encoding the categoricals (one-hot
`occupation` and `marital`), since the model needs numbers.

::: {#real-load .cell execution_count=10}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import pandas as pd

credit = datasets.load_credit()
y_r = credit["income_high"].to_numpy().astype(float)   # target: 1 if income > $50k
s_r = credit["sex"].to_numpy().astype(float)           # protected: 1 = male
X_r = credit.drop(columns=["income_high", "sex"])      # proxies — sex DROPPED
print(f"{len(credit):,} rows · X columns (sex dropped): {list(X_r.columns)}")

# the only lab-local step: one-hot the categoricals, then standardize for the fit
X_enc = pd.get_dummies(X_r, columns=["occupation", "marital"], drop_first=True).to_numpy().astype(float)
X_z = (X_enc - X_enc.mean(0)) / (X_enc.std(0) + 1e-9)   # z-score each proxy column
print(f"encoded proxy matrix: {X_z.shape}")
```

```
30,000 rows · X columns (sex dropped): ['age', 'education_years', 'hours_per_week', 'occupation', 'marital']
encoded proxy matrix: (30000, 15)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Where This Data Comes From
The ACS decode, the `income_high` target, the protected `sex` attribute, and the
proxy leak through `occupation` are built and owned **once** in
[The Income & Fairness Dataset](../../data/06-the-credit-dataset.qmd).  This lab
reloads that prepared `(X, y, s)` with the one-line recipe above and never
re-derives it; the only lab-local step is one-hot encoding the categoricals, as
that page's contract allows.
:::

Train a plain scorecard on the proxies (a logistic fit — `sex` is not among its
inputs), then run the **same** penalised fit on its score, feeding the protected
`sex` as the variable to neutralise.  We are checking two things: the **parity
gap** (how much higher the average predicted score is for men than for women — it
should be near zero if the model is fair) and the **CKA** between the prediction
and `sex` (how much the prediction still depends on the group).  CKA needs an
$n\times n$ table of pairwise similarities, which is too big for all 30,000 rows, so
we read CKA on a ~2000-row sample; the parity gap is read on the full panel.

::: {#real-fit .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(X_z, y_r)   # scorecard — sex DROPPED from inputs
base_score: Float[Array, "n"] = clf.predict_proba(X_z)[:, 1]   # P(high income | proxies)

pred_plain = fair_fit(base_score, y_r, s_r, mu=0.0)     # plain — proxy leak intact
pred_fair = fair_fit(base_score, y_r, s_r, mu=8.0)      # same tool, penalty on

def parity_gap(p: Float[Array, "n"]) -> float:
    """Demographic-parity gap: mean prediction for men − for women."""
    return float(p[s_r == 1].mean() - p[s_r == 0].mean())   # P̄(male) − P̄(female)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = rng.choice(len(y_r), 2000, replace=False)         # subsample only for the O(n²) CKA
print(f"            parity gap   CKA(pred, sex)")
print(f"plain        {parity_gap(pred_plain):+.3f}        {cka_rbf(pred_plain[idx], s_r[idx]):.3f}")
print(f"CKA penalty  {parity_gap(pred_fair):+.3f}        {cka_rbf(pred_fair[idx], s_r[idx]):.3f}   ← gap closes")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
            parity gap   CKA(pred, sex)
plain        +0.120        0.035
CKA penalty  +0.005        0.010   ← gap closes
```
:::
:::

bins = np.linspace(0, 1, 31)
for ax, pred, ttl in [(axL, pred_plain, "plain scorecard"),
                      (axR, pred_fair, "CKA penalty (λ=8)")]:
    ax.hist(pred[s_r == 0], bins=bins, color=WARM, alpha=0.55, density=True, label="women")
    ax.hist(pred[s_r == 1], bins=bins, color=COOL, alpha=0.55, density=True, label="men")
    ax.axvline(pred[s_r == 0].mean(), color=WARM, lw=2)
    ax.axvline(pred[s_r == 1].mean(), color=COOL, lw=2)
    ax.set_title(f"{ttl} · gap={parity_gap(pred):+.2f}", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xlabel("predicted P(high income)"); despine(ax)
axL.set_ylabel("density"); axL.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper right")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

## 💰 Rung 4 · Application — The Accuracy–Fairness Frontier

There is no single "fair model"; there is a **curve**.  The deliverable is the
accuracy–fairness frontier: sweep the penalty weight $\lambda$ from 0 (pure
accuracy) upward, and at each setting read the model's accuracy against its
fairness metric — here the demographic-parity gap (the gap between the average
predicted scores of the two groups).  Each point on the curve is one $\lambda$
setting, showing what accuracy and what gap it buys.  The frontier lays out the
trade-off, so you can pick the smallest $\lambda$ that meets your fairness threshold
and *see* what it costs.

::: {#frontier-sweep .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code}
sweep = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0, 8.0, 20.0]
acc, gap, cka_dep = [], [], []
print(f"{'λ':>6}  {'accuracy':>9}  {'parity gap':>11}  {'CKA(pred,sex)':>14}")
print("-" * 46)
for lam in sweep:
    p = fair_fit(base_score, y_r, s_r, mu=lam)
    a = ((p > 0.5).astype(int) == y_r).mean()            # classification accuracy at 0.5
    g = abs(parity_gap(p))                               # |demographic-parity gap|
    c = cka_rbf(p[idx], s_r[idx])                        # the kernel dependence
    acc.append(a); gap.append(g); cka_dep.append(c)
    print(f"{lam:>6g}  {a:>9.3f}  {g:>11.3f}  {c:>14.3f}")
```

::: {#fig-frontier-compute .cell execution_count=14}
``` {.python .cell-code}
gap_arr: Float[Array, "n_sweep"] = np.array(gap)   # |parity gap| at each λ
acc_arr: Float[Array, "n_sweep"] = np.array(acc)   # accuracy at each λ

# the elbow = the sweep point farthest from the chord joining the two endpoints
gap_u = (gap_arr - gap_arr.min()) / (np.ptp(gap_arr) + 1e-9)   # rescale both axes to [0,1]
acc_u = (acc_arr - acc_arr.min()) / (np.ptp(acc_arr) + 1e-9)
start: Float[Array, "2"] = np.array([gap_u[0], acc_u[0]])      # one endpoint of the chord
chord: Float[Array, "2"] = np.array([gap_u[-1] - gap_u[0], acc_u[-1] - acc_u[0]])
chord = chord / np.linalg.norm(chord)                          # unit chord direction

offsets: Float[Array, "n_sweep 2"] = np.column_stack([gap_u, acc_u]) - start
proj: Float[Array, "n_sweep"] = einx.dot("p i, i -> p", offsets, chord)   # offset · chord
dist = np.linalg.norm(offsets - proj[:, None] * chord, axis=1)   # ⟂ distance of each point to the chord
knee = int(np.argmax(dist))                                    # the elbow = the farthest point
print(f"elbow at λ = {sweep[knee]:g}  (parity gap {gap_arr[knee]:.3f}, accuracy {acc_arr[knee]:.3f})")
```

There it is: a curve you can stake a policy on.  The same penalty — minimise
$\text{fit} + \lambda\cdot\operatorname{CKA}(\hat y, S)$, with CKA the very
double-centering you met measuring distance correlation — read a toy group-shift, a
nonlinear proxy hole, and finally real Census income, escalating only the data and
never the tool.  At the top it hands back not a verdict but a **frontier**: pick the
smallest $\lambda$ that clears your fairness bar, and the curve tells you exactly
what accuracy you pay for it.  Scaling this penalty end to end on the full feature
set — and reporting the gap before and after on the real scorecard — is the job
[Job B · Neutralize an Income Model](lab-jobB-neutralize-credit.qmd) takes up next.
